blocks.text: The SDLC is an organized method for developing software that ensures it meets quality standards and functions properly. Software developers and engineers use it to guide the design, development and testing of software. The SDLC consists of several stages (Fig. 1.1), and each stage has distinct tasks and goals: requirement gathering, analysis, design, coding or implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance.

blocks.alt: Top left: six SDLC stages from Requirement to Maintenance stepping down like stairs with arrows forward and feedback arrows back. Top right: the six Waterfall phases in strict sequence. Bottom: a circular Agile cycle of requirements, design, development, testing, deployment and review with notes on practices, benefits and limits.
blocks.caption: The SDLC stages, the Waterfall model and the Agile cycle (original diagram after Figures 1.1 to 1.3).
blocks.long_description: The software development life cycle moves through requirement, analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance, and a stage can feed back to the one before it. The Waterfall model runs the same kind of phases strictly in order, finishing each before the next and not going back, which is simple but inflexible. Agile instead repeats a short cycle of requirements, design, development, testing, deployment and review, delivering small working parts quickly and taking feedback after every cycle.

items: Requirement gathering: understand and collect what the software must do.
Design: plan how the software will look and work.
Deployment: make the software available to users.
Maintenance: keep it working and up to date.

blocks.prompt: Why is the SDLC used by software developers?
blocks.explanation: It is an organized method that guides design, development and testing step by step, so the software meets quality standards and works properly; each stage has clear tasks and goals.

items: SDLC: organized method guiding design, development and testing so software meets quality standards.
Stages: requirement gathering, (analysis), design, development, testing, deployment, maintenance (Fig. 1.1).
